name: building-a-homestead
description: Building a Homestead: building a house from the ground up, raising farm animals, and growing your own crops, detailed enough to actually go out and do it. The building half opens on the thesis that most building failures are not engineering failures but coordination failures at the boundaries between disciplines and between design and construction, then works through site and ground investigation and why sampling a handful of points is what you are really doing, orientation and solar design, foundations from strip footings to frost-line bearing and the expansive-clay case, the gravity system and the lateral system treated separately, shear walls and hold-downs and why a partially built structure has no lateral system at all, a five-way comparison of timber frame against masonry, reinforced concrete, mass timber and steel, then the envelope where buildings actually fail: the four control layers in the order of importance that is itself the content -- water, air, vapour, thermal -- flashing, drying potential and why a wall with a vapour barrier on both sides cannot dry and will fail, roofs and ponding, concrete mix and cover and curing, wood moisture content and movement, steel, masonry movement joints, building services, fire safety, construction sequencing, codes and permitting, and a build checklist. The livestock half covers ruminant digestion and volatile fatty acids and why cattle are different, nutrient requirements, species selection with gestation and characteristics for cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry, housing and fencing, herd health and biosecurity including FAMACHA and refugia, reproduction and breeding and EPDs and dystocia, grazing management from continuous to rotational to mob with the trade-off of each, stocking rate against stocking density, Animal Units, body condition scoring, and the Five Freedoms with low-stress handling. The crop half covers soil science and cation exchange capacity, fertility management, crop production and growing degree days, rotation and the several jobs it does at once, integrated pest management and economic thresholds, irrigation methods compared on efficiency and cost and limitation, an honest assessment of conventional, organic, regenerative and no-till systems, and a growing checklist -- plus a glossary and the books, codes and free extension services that actually teach this.
